utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. We are sitting in a different courtroom, in the absence of Judge Lattanzi and Mr. Harvey. Judge Lattanzi will not be with us today, so we are sitting pursuant to 15 bis, and I take it Mr. Harvey's attending another courtroom. That said, let's continue, Mr. Karadzic. We'll give our ruling after the first break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, General, we went through some documents in relation to things that you participated in, yourself. Today, we haven't really got much time, so I'd just like to deal with some things very briefly; actually, certain documents concerning phenomena that you are familiar with. Believe me, no objections are being raised towards anyone. We simply want to paint a picture for the Trial Chamber to see what we were up against and what we had to resolve at the time. I'd like to deal with the issue of water and power supply, primarily of the city of Sarajevo. I would like to call up 1D214, please. Oh, we've had that.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there's no document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 193.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has been admitted as Exhibit D453.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we're not going to dwell on it too long. This is a government session of the 7th of August. I just wanted us to see what the situation was like just before you arrived. So could we please have the second page and 3. We're going to see it in English as well, and 3. It's got to be the next page in English. Can we scroll down a bit in English. Or, actually, is it the page before this one? I assume it's got to be the page between this one and the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just waited, but did the general attend that government session? Is there any point of putting this document to the witness? Or just you can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the government charged its ministers with co-operating on matters that UNPROFOR was interested in; Mrs. Plavsic, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I don't really have to read all this out. It has to do with power supply. It's not only a humanitarian thing; it's also a major economic problem, and that is what it says here. The transmission lines are down, and also since there is a war situation -- well, actually, we're still dealing with this "AD-3," and it says: [In English] "... the task ..." [Interpretation] So the government had assigned that task to work on these particular matters. Can we have the next page in English and in Serbian. General, I'd just like to show that when you arrived, those problems were already there, and efforts were being made to overcome the situation as it was. AD-8, please, could we see that now. I'm sorry, it was somewhere else: "The government asked the ministries to make sure that the resources it has are not used as means of war, except that we will be compelled to do that if the enemy side continues to behave the way they have been behaving so far." So this has been admitted. Do you know, General, that Biljana Plavsic managed to get constant support from the government, from the Ministries of Energy and Water Management in order to keep her promise to you? I mean what she promised to the United Nations. When I say "promised you," I mean, it's not you, personally, it's the UN.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, when you talk about the government, what government do you mean? Do you mean the Bosnian government or the Serbian leadership government?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we, the Serbs in Bosnia, had an assembly and the Presidency, and we had a government as the executive. Since Mrs. Plavsic committed herself to various things when she had discussions with the UN, then she presented that to the government, and then the Serb government -- not the Presidency, not the Assembly. The Serb government, that's a separate organ. She then -- well, she made an effort to carry out everything that she had committed herself to. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure, as you mentioned, Mr. Karadzic, that when we first started or work, the power was down, there was no -- there were no water supplies and no services, and I know that those services are humane in nature. I know that there were so many casualties receiving treatment at the hospitals, and I -- and hospitals needed power supply urgently. I personally -- along with my staff members, I said that we should try to appease things, try to do some humanitarian work in order to restore water and power. So we agreed, after long talks with both sides, Mr. Ganic, Mrs. Plavsic, and the concerned ministers, we all agreed to provide -- to set up what we call working group where technicians and engineers could sit on, those who are experienced in restoring water supplies and power supplies in the city. The working group met once at the airport, and we were able, thanks to our co-ordination with this group, with the members of the group - I'm talking about the technicians and the engineers - we were able to restore the power supply, but only for a day or a day and a half. And I remember that we did celebrate the occasion at the United Nations. We were extremely happy for the event. However, there were some reparations in the area next to Litra [phoen], but that area came under fire, the group came under fire, and they had to withdraw and rush to the PTT building. They told me that they came under fire and the area came under fire and there was a power failure once again. So in terms of principle, yes, negotiations were fruitful and, as I said, that we always came up with very hopeful -- with results that provided grounds for hope. However, things were -- to me, were different in the field. I know that I was met with understanding and with co-operation from the officials at both sides, the Serbian side and the Bosnian side. And as I said, the problem lies with the lower-rank leaders or officials.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Since this has been admitted, could I now have 65 ter 202. Actually, I just took an example of a government session prior to your arrival, a session dealing with that, whereas this document is from the 10th of October. Could we have page 9 as soon as we actually get the document. 65 ter 202. Then AD-41, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document we are seeing is the 52nd session on 22nd of September. I think you got the number wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 26th of September, the 52nd session. Yes, 22. Now this seems to be something different. Actually, 202, is that it? 65 ter 202, that should be it. However, that's not what it says here. We need 65 ter 202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is it. Why don't we show the first page to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please identify the first page. Oh, this is the 45th session. In Serbian, it's fine, but it's wrong in English. In Serbian, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on the other side we have the 8th of August, and we've dealt with that already. It's already been admitted. Right now, we have the right page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I remember you said "10th of October." Is this the right document, Mr. Karadzic? Then move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, we have the right document. Actually, it was written down -- the minutes were compiled on the 10th of October, but see up here, the date, "Pale," the 10th. Could we please have AD-41; page 9 in Serbian. Sorry, 42, 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention, General, to 42. I'm also drawing it to the attention of all the participants. However, the English page will have to be changed in the meantime: "The government described the drinking water supplies problem in the municipalities of the Sarajevo region as a delicate and acute one, saying that measures should be taken to resolve the problem, especially before the coming raining season: "It has been concluded that resources should be provided for the disinfection of reservoirs and the waterworks, particularly in relation to the region of Igman." As you know, Igman was under Muslim control at the time, but as far as the water is concerned, the government is looking at the city as a whole; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When we were talking about restoring water and power supplies, we were talking about the entire city and not about -- and the entire region, Sarajevo and the surroundings, and not only the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, yes, you're right, the region of Sarajevo. It also says that: "It was concluded that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska should be informed about this so that the army could plan its military operations, while bearing in mind the problems presented in the documents." So this is from the government session. Before your stay and as soon as you arrived, great attention was paid to water supplies, not only for the Serb-held areas, but the general area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, unless it is objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now please have 65 ter 204. 65 ter 204, this is a government session held on the 2nd of October, so it's from the 2nd of October and the other one was the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] AD-19. In Serbian, it's page 5, and in English, it's either 5 or 6. So when we see paragraph 19, we will realise -- I'll read it again before we get the English: "The government took note of the Information," with a capital I, so I guess it's some kind of a document, "on supplying municipal centres in Republika Srpska with drinking water, as well as prospects of providing water to critical areas, with special attention being paid to the region of Sarajevo." So it's basically at the very next session. Actually, that was the 52nd session, and this is the 54th session. The government assigned this to someone, and this someone provided this document, acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you see that the government is dealing with the issue of water and electricity at each and every one of the sessions, and there is no distinction made between the Serb-held areas and the Muslim-held areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it -- I have to note that it was translated in the English version as point reference 18. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nineteen is missing in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it isn't. It's translated as 18, point 18. If you could read 18, then you could confirm that it is point 19 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're right. It was called 18 here. Actually, if we scroll down, we may see that there are two paragraphs number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not trying to say that the government could have done all of this, but don't you agree that the government was paying attention to this? You talked about the leadership. The government is a bit below the Presidency, but you see that the government constantly had this on its agenda?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I mentioned in my reports that we came to an agreement with the parties concerned on the necessity to restore the infrastructure of the city and the surroundings of the city. We came to an agreement on that, and the other party -- or the parties expressed enthusiasm on performing that. But I once again say that we do come to an agreement with the governments, with the delegations, with the leaders. However, when these agreements are or were to be implemented on the ground, those agreements were met with violence in the field. That was the situation all the time. We came to agreements, there was positive atmosphere that prevailed on the talks, the talks provided grounds for hopes, but when the groups on the ground, those who were charged with the implementation, used to come under fire and used to be compelled to withdraw, and we all started -- we all the time started at scratch. I do not deny that there was sincere desire expressed by the parties to come to an agreement. We set up a working group composed of specialists and experts, working alongside and along with experts from the United Nations. However, the implementation of the agreements was met with violence on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are tested as to our French proficiency, but I think it's been sorted out. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D513, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we are just going to look at two very briefly, and perhaps we are going to tender as associated exhibits other documents, if the Trial Chamber and the OTP allow that. Could we now have 65 ter number 205. Yes, that's the document. Could we please look at AD-40, AD-40. I would like to draw your attention to AD-40. I need the following page in the English version, please. The top of the following page, please, the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The government was briefed on the terms which have been required regarding the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. These include supplying electricity, water, gas, and PTT services to the city. "The responsible ministries are due to name experts who would assist Biljana Plavsic in negotiations mediated by UNPROFOR with the opposite side." This is in the Bileca region. In other words, Mrs. Plavsic undertook all the necessary measures in order to receive the government's support and experts who would be able to implement the project. Of course, they could not always prevent fire being opened in the field, but would you agree with me that at the government level, Mrs. Plavsic was successful in securing the government's support for all that you had previously agreed?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mrs. Plavsic was enthusiastic in restoring the infrastructure, and she said that that was in the very own interests of her people. And, of course, she -- her position was positive on the measures, and there was a joint working group that we set up alongside with experts from UNPROFOR. I do not deny her enthusiasm. However, I wasn't privy to her co-ordination with the government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. I just want to demonstrate that we did not make things more difficult intentionally. Our success, however, depended on combat activities --

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't get the translation either. So now do you follow me, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your last question, or you can continue your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has the document been admitted, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D514.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the Court please produce 65 ter 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, General: My intention is to demonstrate that the system and the government never intentionally make things more difficult. However, their success depended on the situation on the ground and combat activities which were either under somebody's control or totally out of anybody's control. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I stated that clearly, and I made my point clear to both sides, the Serbs and the Bosnians. I said to both sides that, We have excellent agreements here, we reached agreement on several issues, but these agreements -- the instructions do not find their way to the foot soldiers. Otherwise, why are we finding ourselves in this situation? We can spend all our time exchanging pleasantries, drinking, eating, but, in fact, nothing is being implemented on the ground, and that is affecting the work of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are looking at 65 ter 212, the 62nd session of the government, held on the 26th of January. Could the court please produce AD-19. In the Serbian version, it will be on page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, before we deal with the question by the accused: You said that: "... but, in fact, nothing is being implemented on the ground, and that is affecting the work of UNPROFOR." What do you think, General, was the reason for such non-implementation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that specific point in time, UNPROFOR was trying to help to restore basic necessities to the city; water, electricity, gas. And that's what we tried to raise with the leaderships from both sides. But all efforts to implement the work were affected by military operations, sniping, shelling. It proved practically impossible for technical teams to reach the locations. There were maps of the locations that needed to be treated, where electricity generators or transformers were located to be repaired. The problems that we confronted were with the junior commanders, the commanders on the ground. We -- I always made the point clear to the leaderships from both sides that it does not serve the purpose to sit at meeting tables, have pleasantries, and not be able to translate these actions into work on the ground, and the world is watching us and criticising us for standing idle, not doing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the leadership was disingenuous or the subordinate commanders were not complying with orders from the leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said over and over again, from day one after I arrived, the negotiations at the higher levels, with Mr. Izetbegovic, with Mr. Ganic at other occasions, with Mr. Karadzic, with his deputies and assistants, sometimes - I did not say all times - I addressed them and underscored the importance of imposing more control, more discipline, on the ground troops, because the ground troops, the lower ranks and commanders and the foot soldiers, the civilian militias, were aggressive, were hostile, and I had the feeling at the time that these -- that the rank and file were not receiving clear instructions, were not being disciplined and told what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could I draw to your attention the fact that the record states from 26 of January. You were still there. Under 16, you can see that the government asked information and received information for direct contribution of Republika Srpska and, in principle, supported all the proposed measures. The government was of the opinion that supplying electricity to the city is a priority task and that all measures should be undertaken to resolve this problem as soon as possible. According to the opinion of the government, transmission lines had to be built as a priority, and especially those that provided supply of electricity to Romanija, Krajina, and Posavina region, including Sarajevo. The protection of transmission lines is also mandatory. The government also imposed the need to carry out full co-operation between competent republican bodies, organisation, municipalities, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down in reading. Bear in mind that your words should be interpreted into the Egyptian based upon the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. I'm under the pressure of time. That's why I'm a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, General, do you see that the problem of supplying this city with electricity, as well as supplying the city with water, is present across the entire territory, both in Republika Srpska as well as in the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question or what? Sir, it was abundantly clear that the problem applied across the board. But in my situation, I am in charge of the Sarajevo -- or I was in charge of Sarajevo Sector, and when I met with leaderships from both sides, we were trying to bring about a degree of calm to allow the technical teams to restore the basic services, but that could not have been done without starting by demilitarisation. And once that was achieved in Sarajevo, being a strategic point in the conflict -- the idea was to start with Sarajevo and to restore normal life, and then the same approach, the same model, could be applied -- could be extended to other areas. That was the principle of the UNPROFOR objective or the principle objective, and that was part of what was known as the Morillon Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My idea, General, sir, was this: I wanted to present to everybody in the courtroom that the problem was omnipresent, that it was not a problem that was confined to Sarajevo, although since you were in Sarajevo, what was going on in Sarajevo was somewhat closer to you. Could the document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D515, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the court please produce 1D2129. We will see what the Sarajevo newspaper "Oslobodjenje" wrote about the problems that existed on the ground. Could the court please produce just the first column. Can it be blown up. I am going to be reading because we don't have a translation yet. This is the Sarajevo-based "Oslobodjenje," on the Muslim side. There were actually two newspapers under the same name "Oslobodjenje." And it says here: "A message arrived from the War Presidency around 11.00 yesterday at the address of the public company water supply and waterworks." The letter was signed by Nedeljko Prstojevic, and in the letter it is stated that: "The commission has decided to discontinue the supply of water to Ilidza and the city of Sarajevo from the locality called Bacevo. The reason for that was the constant shelling of Ilidza and especially the area of water supply, which caused major damage to the pumps and barrels." It is also stated that: "With this regard, the necessary measures were being undertaken in order to protect people and facilities which are in the function of water supply in the area." Finally, there is also a promise: "The water supply will be reinstated after all the damage has been removed." Predrag Lukac goes on to say how convincing the reasons are, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the water supply depends on the electricity supply and that the area of Bacevo was, indeed, under constant shelling and under constant fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's exactly what I said. We know fully well that the two services, water and electricity, are interconnected. And if you remember correctly, the meetings centered on these issues, and when you met with technicians from the UN, in my premise, these were the issues that they raised. But, again, when we reach agreement on what these teams should do, once they go to the location intended for repair work, they end up -- they end up being shelled, snipers were all over the place, and these teams found it impossible to work in these conditions. I called for another meeting, and we sit down, re-discuss the issue, but then when it comes to implementation, it becomes practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you will still agree with me that Sarajevo did get some water and some electricity with the UNPROFOR's assistance. You will agree with me that there was, after all, some water and some electricity at all times. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said we succeeded, and I remember that certain residential areas of Sarajevo got electricity, and you could see the lights all over the place. And, as I said, it was a big -- there was a big celebration. The following day, other areas were intended do come in line for repair work, and when the teams went there, they were targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you said, in the previous answer, that, I quote: "But, again, when we reach agreement on what these terms should do, once they go to the location intended for repair work, they end up -- they end up being shelled, snipers were all over the place, and these teams found it impossible to work in these conditions." Did you know at the time or do you know now from which direction those shells and snipings were coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I go back to the reports that we received from the military observers. We received reports that the shelling or the sniping had come from this side or that side. We have to bear in mind once there is shelling or sniping from one side, then the other side will respond immediately, and we were caught in the middle. We were on the front-line. And even the villages along the front-line, have you one part of the village on the -- under the control of the Bosniaks and the other side of the same village under the Serb control. Therefore, once the shelling or the sniping starts from one side, the other side starts responding, and that's -- that was -- that represented the crux of the problem that we were dealing with. But then, again, that was not the issue that I was trying to make here. The issue I want to make reference to is that work -- repair work stops, and that's why the problem -- that's the problem we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you have your objection, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only point that I would raise at this point in time is that the witness spoke about the event in general terms. He did not actually confirm the event that Prstojevic raised here, the shelling on Ilidza. So he hasn't really dealt with the particular document with this particular reference to the event that was discussed in this first paragraph. That's my only observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general did come to the Serbian part of Ilidza. Hrasnica is also Ilidza, but it is the Muslim part. And he sensed the mood of the people. They welcomed him. And even the president of the municipality promises here that as soon as the damages are repaired, there will be water supply. Maybe the general did not read this copy of "Oslobodjenje," but we are talking about the same types of incidents of the kind that are described in this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The general didn't confirm anything specific which is reflected in this news clipping, and you even didn't ask any question about it. While the general agreed with you, in general terms, we'll not admit this, based upon our consistent guide-line. Let's move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The position of the Defence is that the water supply was not shut down intentionally. It was done because of the damages, which the general confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the court please produce 1D1427.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, while we are waiting for the document: General, do you agree with me that the lack of water and electricity was caused by frequent damages on the infrastructure and installations? Why would repair teams otherwise would have been sent there? Could you agree with me that repair teams were sent to repair the facilities which were damaged as a result of war activities?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as you know, there was a general agreement on the situation in Sarajevo, and this general agreement entailed commitment on the warring parties in the Sarajevo area to create the conditions for the United Nations forces and their support services to allow them to accomplish their duties. And there was an understanding that if there was any military hostilities, then military hostilities should be confined to the front-lines between the warring parties, and that the United Nations would not be caught in the military operations. In our case, we found ourselves caught in the situation, and we found ourselves in confrontation with junior commands. And despite the fact that all the time and effort that was put into trying to reach an agreement with you, with Ms. Plavsic, on the need to restore all these services, on the need for teams to continue their work. And we sat down, we reached agreements, we signed documents, and we provide protection. Before the movement of these teams, prior information is transmitted to the warring parties to make sure that the work group will undertake repair work; yet, we find out that there is an exchange of mortar shells, there is an exchange of sniping, there is an exchange of shelling. But, of course, the facilities -- water and electricity facilities were extensively damaged as a result of the -- and we know that the movement of tracked armour led to extensive destruction to the infrastructure -- to the piping system. This is a natural outcome of hostilities. What we tried to do is to put an end to these military hostilities so that we can provide the services to the Sarajevo area. And it must be noted here that that was part of my mandate, and I took the initiative to try and improve these facilities in that specific region.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, sir. Could the court please produce -- or, rather, will the Trial Chamber change its decision now, at this moment, about the document for admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean to reconsider the non-admission of 1D2129? I think you can do without the document. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the court please produce a short document, sent by Colonel Davout, 1D2147. I'm sure that there must be a translation of this document in existence, 1D2147. Thank you. I don't know if we have an English translation. This is a letter -- yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew Colonel Davout, did you not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, he was my deputy in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this letter, he addresses Mrs. Plavsic, and the subject is "Meeting with UNPROFOR engineers regarding gas": "For a better understanding of all the problems you encounter with regard to the transport and distribution of gas, UNPROFOR Sector engineering is requesting a meeting with specialists from the area with your government. "This meeting could take place in Pale on the 24th or 25th of November, 1992. UNPROFOR will be represented by Major Hebnes." And so on and so forth, copied to Colonel Galic. Obviously, at that level on your side and on the side of Mrs. Plavsic, there was mutual understanding. You understood our difficulties. Was this the customary way your services communicated with Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, any document that came my way would be signed by me. But if we take this date, in particular, I was on leave, and Colonel Davout was in the command at that -- took over the command at that time, and he would continue to implement the policies related to the infrastructure. We had a vision and we had a plan. Had I been there, I would be supervising. However, if I was away, whether on leave or in meetings to the leadership in Zagreb, he would take over, and work never stopped. This was our method of work. When we wanted to convene a meeting, we would send a letter to that effect, and who would be representing us, and asked the relevant parties to inform us who would be their representative, and we would set the time and the date and the points to be discussed at the meeting. This was the method we followed in communication and co-ordination with the relevant parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I take it, General, you do not have any reason to doubt the authenticity of this document signed by Colonel Davout.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. This is a routine procedure in communications with the relevant parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D516, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the practice. I don't think the -- can you keep those two documents as well? Okay. I don't think those two documents are identical, in the sense that each version has its own handwriting. This is the B/C/S version, without Colonel Davout's signature, and this is English. But I take it both are identical, in terms of its content. So can we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. This is a note jotted down by the person who received this document in the Government of Republika Srpska, and he forwarded it further on. I can't really read it, but it says: "UNPROFOR, with regard to all questions, questions of importance," I think. This is a note jotted down by someone from the government who received this and who obviously put it in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what I have to -- yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think these are actually two items that should be exhibited separately, because one is the letter sent, and obviously the translation, and the other one is showing the reception of that letter. So it should actually be two exhibits under two different numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that was my observation, or we can give some branch number or not. I'll leave it in the hands of the Registry. So we'll admit it as two original documents. The numbers will be given.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D516 and D517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, D517 being the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I clarify something here? If they sent us a letter, such as is the case here, if we received such a letter, there is a person who puts a sign or a signal on it to forward it and to indicate to the senior officer what is the procedure. These are internal procedures when we receive official letters. This is always the case with these documents. When a certain letter comes in a formal manner, we copy it, and the copy is signed by the specialised person, indicating to the senior officer what is the usual process in dealing with such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D373, could we have that, please. There is an English version, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, General, let me introduce the document to you. It is an agreement between the Serb commander, General Mladic, and the Croatian chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Brigade General Petkovic, Milivoj Petkovic. So do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. The original is in English and the translation is into Croatian or Serbian. So could we have the English version as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that Serbs and Croats often managed to reach an agreement, and they invited the third party to join in? I would like to tell you that the last four pages of this document are actually the English version of this document. So could we have the English version on the other half of the screen. We've up-loaded them together under the same number. This may be it, but we need the fourth page -- no, the fifth page of this document. That's where the English original starts. Thank you. Could we have the Serbian translation on the other half of the screen. No, it's not possible. Okay, then let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the agreement. The original is in English, and it was done through the mediation of the UNPROFOR Main Staff; right? Do you agree that this is the usual facsimile, "Headquarters, BH Command"?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take the date of this document, we will find that it indicates the peak of the meetings that took place at the airport between the joint committees. Now, for this document, I did not attend any co-ordination meeting among the three parties; Serbs, Croats, and the Bosnian Muslims. At such a level, a meeting was held, except in the joint military committee. That was attended in its opening session by Mr. Mladic, and later on Mr. Gvero was representing him there, and the formula was a formula put in place by General Morillon so that the parties may agree to it. And as you can see, it involved the Morillon Plan to demilitarise the area of Sarajevo and to free the convoys of the United --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let us establish that here, on the first page, we see that General Mladic and General Petkovic signed the document. Right? Did you notice, General, that General Mladic and General Petkovic had signed that document on the first page? Did you notice that, that it had been signed?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we scroll down a bit so that we could see that it has to do with Morillon. No, we actually want to scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this up here? Is this intended for Morillon, this facsimile? Right? You see the handwritten words on the top.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the norm. When we sent letters, we addressed them to a number of parties. And once any document was signed, we received a copy of it at the United Nations. This was the agreement always. And you are aware that the work of the United Nations is always documented, and we have instructions from above to have documentation for all matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I'm not receiving translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Could you repeat your question again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just wanted to draw the attention of all participants to the essence of this document. This is an agreement on the implementation of an area of separation. Then there is a reference to cessation of hostilities throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, freedom of movement, and also renewing/restoring public utilities. Well, first it's the cessation of hostilities, everything that should be done in that respect, then freedom of movement. Could we have the next page in English, please. D. D says: "Restoration of civil utilities." That meant that civil utilities would be restored as well. Under "Cessation of hostilities," there was a reference to the withdrawal of all heavy weapons. That was on the previous page, but I'm sure that everybody saw that. Freedom of movement, restoration of civil utilities. Then on this page, removal of heavy weapons: "All heavy weapons will be withdrawn from the following locations: Mojmilo, Dobrinja, Hrasnica, Butmir, Otes and Stup."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were all under Muslim control; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I forgot to mention Sokolac, Sokolovic Kolonija, Lukavac, Gornji Kotorac, Vojkovici and Nedzarici are under Serb control; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, there is a proposal to set up a joint commission; right? Then this is my handwriting at the bottom of the page: "Our people are sleeping on our side." That is my handwriting. That's what it says. That means that our participants in the work of this joint commission will be sleeping on our side, will be spending the night on our side. Could we now have the second page, please. The next page, please. Control measures that we agreed upon, and the last subparagraph (5): [In English] "The joint commission will establish mixed patrols not later than December 26th, 1992." [Interpretation] Then, in my own hand, it says: "The two in the jeep." And the same thing in the Serbian: "The two in the jeep."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we were always prepared to have Serb policemen on the Serb side, a Serb policeman and an UNPROFOR representative, and on the Muslim side, a Muslim policeman and an UNPROFOR representative?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall well, sir, is that we used to be there as UNPROFOR. General Morillon, and myself, and the chief of staff, and I think it was Brigade General Thompson - he was British, I can't remember his name well - and we would ask, What do you want the parties to do? And we would put down all these points that are written in the document to ask them to implement these and to agree on how implementation should take place through the work of the joint commission. And then we would go into details in our talks; how will we work on restoring the infrastructure and to provide freedom of movement for the convoys. And we would go into details; who would make up the guard group. We had no reservations for representatives of UNPROFOR being there so that no party would believe that other party is spying on their work. We wanted the whole process to be a joint effort, without any suspicions prevailing in the minds of any party. I recall this document exactly, and the points mentioned are the points that we brought up and insisted that they constitute the agenda of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, General, that the implementation of this plan of General Morillon's or this UNPROFOR plan would have meant the end of all the troubles of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we used to pray for this to happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that Izetbegovic -- or, rather, Ganic's side did not sign this and did not accept this?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, we did face some difficulties in this matter. First, Mr. Gvero did not issue his decisions directly. He had to return to his leadership and then come back to us for signing. And then the other party, represented by Colonel Siber, had some reservations on what was in the text. I can't recall what, exactly, but he had some reservations. He would say, Let us start by restoring the infrastructure first, or, Let us start by stopping hostilities, or stopping the shelling, or ending the siege, collecting -- gathering heavy arms under the supervision of UNPROFOR, and then we will start addressing other problems. As I recall, there was a problem as to the priorities, what comes first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before admitting this document, I would like the general to see the entire document. Can we see the next page, or page 9. Do you remember this, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me it's a letter addressed from General Philippe Morillon to Mr. Karadzic. It involved -- it addressed the shelling of the hospital. And I want to clarify a point here. We were very moved -- shocked by this shelling. It was shameful to us all, and everybody in Sarajevo was pleading, the physicians, the population, the hospital being shelled with children and nurseries involved. This was a letter of protest, after we saw the results of the shelling and the sources of this, as observed by the military observers. I did not see this letter, but he told me -- General Morillon told me that he sent a letter of protest to the Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea, General, why this letter was attached to the previous document, while they referred to different dates?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see -- excuse me. I see no link between this document and the document that came before it, because this document is a very special case in an area that was the center of attention to all parties. I do not believe it was attached in any way to the former document that relates to the work of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you agree, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, this last page is a separate matter, I will tell the Defence to delete this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first four pages are in B/C/S, which is also a separate document, so we'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian version is the translated version, and the English is the original. Perhaps one number can be assigned, or two. But, anyway, they should be separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told the Court Deputy was referring to Exhibit D517, which is a separate version in B/C/S of the previous document. We'll admit this in full as Exhibit D518. One more question and we'll have a break, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just by way of information, this letter, sent to me by Morillon, follows another letter, a different one, in much harsher terms, sent to Izetbegovic, because they were provoking Serbian fire. General Morillon liked to scold both sides, although you could see who caused what. Could we please have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01187.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, if you recall, that agreement between General Mladic and General Petkovic was signed on the 22nd of December, and this is what happened on the 23rd of December. This is a report for that entire day from 1800 hours. So let us focus our attention on where the enemy artillery was operating from. It says: "Strong attacks. Fierce offensive activity on the north and western sector of the front." And then it says 110 shells on the Hadzici area, 60 shells on the Ilidza area, around 50 shells on the Rajlovac area, 120 shells on Vogosca and Semizovac, and 70 on Ilidza. I would like to draw your attention to number 3: "Four civilians were killed and three were wounded by enemy artillery fire. Great material damage was caused to civilian facilities in the areas of Hadzici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca and Ilijas." Do you agree, General, that this was no contribution to peace? As a matter of fact, this was some kind of response to that agreement that had been reached on the previous day? This made it obvious that nothing would come out of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I recall well that after this agreement was signed, and in the next meeting there was early shelling since early hours of the morning, and I and General Morillon were waiting for the delegations, and he laughed and said, This is how agreements are implemented. He was being cynical. I repeat, I do not know now exactly which party started with the shelling or what's the number of those killed or wounded on this side or that, but all I can say is, and I'll repeat this once again, whenever we met, there were fine words about peace and the desire for co-operation and for leading UN operations to success. We heard fine words from leaders, and I'm repeating this again. I seem to be repeating myself over and over. Nice words from the leaders. We agree on points. Yes, they say they want to achieve this, they want to help us in achieving this. Then we come to the ground and we find something totally different, and this was always the problem. Your Honour, this was always the problem. And this is not what I say only, but all those who worked with me have the same to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page, just to see the signature and the losses sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that four civilians got killed, three were wounded. Less combatants were killed or wounded. This is a document of General Galic's. However, General, do you agree that it wasn't the Croats that violated the cease-fire? This fire came from Izetbegovic's positions, the positions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina under Halilovic's control?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Mustafa Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mustafa was Hajrulahovic.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Hajrulahovic, I know him. [Interpretation] I am going to repeat what I have already said. We do agree, and then there is fire, and we receive reports about the source of their fire. We tell them that, You were the source of fire, and that was according to the reports of the observers. But they denied the reports. They would say they were not the side that fired the shells. So the question was always being asked, Who was -- who was starting? That was the situation all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted as Exhibit D519. And we'll have a break for 30 minutes. We'll resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're glad to see you back, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Much happier here, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I heard that, Mr. Karadzic, you have something to raise some the absence of the witness, or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I will raise the issue. I am concerned that we have a witness through whom I would like to present some very valuable documents, and I don't have enough time to clarify with the witness what he meant when he issued certain oral statements. I have to kindly request to be given one whole session. I did not cover the whole ground and, of course, I cannot recall this witness, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't follow you. When you said you cannot recall this witness, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah, recalled. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, how much would you need, albeit prematurely, for your redirect examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if nothing else for redirect arises, I would have only to address one particular small matter, and it relates to the letter that Monsieur Morillon sent on the 31st of January. And it's rather more a formality because the witness has dealt with this particular document, responded to it. Therefore, the Prosecution would like to have that exhibited separately. That's the only matter that I have at the moment. Otherwise, no redirect so far. But I just want to mention one point. The consistent feature of the witness was -- all over the days now was is that he had to say, As I have said already, and, I repeat myself, and, Again I repeat myself. A lot of time was wasted asking the same issues over and over again. That's just an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you have had four hours and 40 minutes so far with this witness. So, accordingly, you would have 20 minutes left for your cross-examination. But given the situation, and technical difficulties we have had, and translation as well, we'll give you an hour from now. So please try your best to conclude your cross-examination in an hour's time from now. Taking advantage of the absence of the witness, the Chamber is minded to issue its ruling regarding the request made yesterday, on behalf of Mr. Karadzic, to postpone the cross-examination of the next witness, Mr. Suljevic, until after the recess in order to allow him to prepare. This request was based, firstly, on the recent disclosure of certain documents relevant to the witness, pursuant to a Rule 66(B) request, and on the fact that the Prosecution has recently indicated that it would seek to tender 45 documents through the witness by way of an additional recently-prepared Rule 92 ter statement. The Chamber notes, once again, that when Rule 66(B) requests are made relatively close in time to the testimony of a particular witness, the accused cannot use the subsequent disclosure of Rule 66(B) material in accordance with that request as a basis for requesting the postponement of the testimony or of the cross-examination of that witness, when the Prosecution has responded to the Rule 66(B) request in a timely manner. Nonetheless, if the documents in question are important to the testimony of a particular witness, there may be circumstances in which the Chamber would grant more time to the accused to prepare for his cross-examination. The Chamber also notes that Mr. Karadzic was put on notice that the 45 documents in question were intended to be used with Mr. Suljevic during his statement -- during his testimony in early June 2010. What is new, however, is the statement produced by the Prosecution in which the witness describes or comments on each of those documents. The Prosecution has indicated that it would seek to tender this statement and the exhibits in lieu of asking the witness about the exhibits in the courtroom. This statement was only provided to the accused and the Chamber on 19th July 2010. In light of the timing of the provision of this statement to the accused, the Chamber has decided that it will not be admitted, and the Prosecution should rather address the documents described in it with the witness in the courtroom during his direct examination, and seek to tender those it considers necessary in this manner. That said, Mr. Karadzic, given the Chamber will not be admitting this new statement describing the 45 documents in lieu of oral testimony from the witness in relation to them, we do not consider it necessary to postpone your cross-examination of Mr. Suljevic. We also consider it unnecessary at this stage to grant additional time for your cross-examination, as the number of documents being tendered through this witness, whether pursuant to Rule 92 ter or otherwise, was taken into consideration by the Chamber in determining the time available to you for your cross-examination. But we will keep this matter under review as we hear his evidence. We note, in this regard, that it may not be possible, given the remaining time available today and tomorrow, to finish your cross-examination of Mr. Suljevic before the recess. You would, in that event, have time over the recess to prepare the remainder of your cross-examination. We'll bring in the witness. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. While we're doing that, I could indicate that we won't have any objection to the 31st of January, 1993, letter. So if the Prosecutor just wants to have that admitted without asking any further questions, I think that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have up-loaded this document separately just now into e-court, and it would have the 65 ter number 90184, and that's the exact document. And I ask for admittance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have no objection to the suggestion by Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I think that's the most practical way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted as Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would recommend or suggest to the Chamber that the document is associated with the D351. The source was the same, and that was an attempt by General Morillon to strike a balance. It's about the same incident, and the letters were sent to two different addressees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no doubt you'll have another opportunity to tender that document through proper witnesses or through Bar table motion. Apologies for your inconvenience, General. We had some administrative matters to deal with in your absence. We'll try our best to conclude your examination in an hour's time from now. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce 1D2123, 1D2123.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document to be produced, General, sir, let me tell you something about the contents of the document. I suppose that the document originates from you and describes your meeting with myself and Colonel Siber. Do you agree, General, that you reached the Serbian leadership in an easier way than the top leadership of the Muslims? Colonel Siber was not my par on the Muslim side, was he, or was he not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, according to my experience in dealing with the parties, you were the party that we dealt with in most matters. And, frankly speaking, we did have some difficulty in talking with General Galic in some civilian affairs. On the other side, we did meet to discuss civil matters with what is called the Presidency, represented by Mr. Gubovic [phoen] or Mr. Ganic. As for military matters, we used to refer to Colonel Siber, and I think he was mandated by the Presidency to negotiate with us on the details of things concerning the shelling, the weapons, and the roadblocks, et cetera, et cetera. But I didn't have any problem reaching an understanding or communicating with any party. Just upon a short notice, we would determine -- set a date for the meeting, and we would meet easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm convinced that the document will show that you were more successful with the Serbs than with the federation. Could you please look at the document. The document describes your meeting with me and then with Colonel Siber on the 13th of December, 1992, which means three weeks after your arrival; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In light of the date of the document, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try and just provide yes-and-no answers. Does it say here that you were reporting back to the Main Staff of UNPROFOR and General Nambiar that I had confirmed that all the heavy weaponry was deployed at 11 locations around Sarajevo? You insisted that that included 120-millimetre mortars, and that I was agreeable to that, or, rather, 82, although I thought that the 82-millimetre mortars, as well as the 60-millimetre mortars, were infantry weaponry, rather than artillery. I also accepted your proposal that armed infantry should observe the artillery weapons and locations, but I was also of the opinion that Egyptian soldiers, for their own safety rather than for our own prejudices, because we did not have any prejudices against you, that they shouldn't be deployed there. You can see all that. And will you agree with me that I offered "kiseonik" [phoen] or, rather, oxygen to be delivered to hospitals via the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did report to headquarters, in details, the contents of our talks, and everything mentioned in this document was reported according to what you said to me in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree in the original document, drafter by Minister Hogg, Douglas Hogg, the word used was "supervision," and not "control," and that you agreed for all that to be supervision, rather than control? That's bullet point 2.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you do remember, sir, that I -- that my position was specific. I told you that I was expert on verification. I was part of a mission for a year in Angola on that particular matter. So I do not want to raise too many technical points, in terms of definitions, whether you're talking about supervision or control. So all what we meant and all what was understood from your statements and declarations that were reported to me, that I verified, myself, in the media, that you were ready to collect such weapons under the control or the monitoring of United Nations forces. So, for me -- control for me, in order to be successful, was to collect the heavy weapons where they were deployed in the 11 positions, and to take them to specific areas so that they can be monitored or controlled by the United Nations. So it was difficult for us to deploy forces all over the positions, to monitor firing from all positions. That was impossible. So the interpretation of those terms meant to collect those weapons in 11 positions, and that those arms should continue to be under Serb control. But I was saying that they should be gathered in 11 positions where cease-fire was observed to make it easier for us to control them and monitor them. So my opinion on that matter was that we would not practically be able to see through to that agreement because the number of observers was very limited. So, as I told you, we used soldiers from the battalions, that we used to train them for a number of weeks on monitoring and controlling matters, and they were assigned to control the various positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely so. However, I did not question the UNPROFOR's position. I just wanted to remind you that the other side wanted UNPROFOR to control, rather than to supervise, and our soldiers wouldn't accept that. And that's why all agreed that the control would be Serb and that supervision would be yours; am I right, sir? And can we move on to the second page?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I exacted said. We were not to assume control -- a control mission of all the weapons, because that needed our many experts, but we wanted for these weapons to be collected or gathered in some specific areas so that we -- our mission to control them would be facilitated and to prevent -- or to see to it that those weapons were not used to fire shells against the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to bullet point 5, describing your meeting with Colonel Siber? Everybody can read, so I don't want to read myself. However, my point of concern is this: [In English] "... the possibility of heavy fighting near the airport in the next days." [Interpretation] How did Colonel Siber know that there might be fighting if the situation was not under his control?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, sir, I'm not talking about the intentions here. I report to my headquarters what the parties have said. I am not discussing the question of intentions. I sincerely report what happened to me, word for word, to my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is precisely what I meant. Your reporting was fair. However, I'm concerned with the fact that he knew in advance that there would be fighting. I, myself, never knew that. Can we look at bullet point 8, where he informed you that what you had discussed would be considered at a higher -- or, rather, at the highest level. You see, you had much more success with the Serbs. You were received by the highest level immediately, whereas Colonel Siljeg [as interpreted] had to go to a higher level after your initial meeting. Just yes or no. He did not have the final say; am I right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and that goes for Mr. Galic. That was a major problem. That's why I always asked to meet the higher leadership. You were always busy, and Mrs. Plavsic was always there. On the other side, I didn't want to waste my time with the leaders on the ground. Of course, they were well-intended, but they had so many complaints and so many allegations and we wasted our time discussing such claims. We had specific targets behind our talks. That's why we came to you, personally. And when you were present, you did receive us, and when you were not there, you were represented by Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And someone else that the interpreters did not catch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for Colonel Siber, I think you were aware of the system there. They would receive the points on military affairs raised by us. They would take these points to their headquarters. I don't think there are officers who are fully mandated to take decisions concerning strategic or political affairs, and that is the case everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the interview, we agreed did we not, that the civilian authorities also had to consult their military structures as to what was acceptable and what was unacceptable from the point of view of security. And do you agree, in that sense, since I was a civilian physician, I also had to consult with my Main Staff and ask them whether a proposal was acceptable from the point of view of security for our troops? Can you please say just yes or no? I'm sure that you can answer by just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, you have all the right to do so. I know that things happened that way, that civilian or political leaders would consult with their military structures, or economic structures, or any other matter. You have the right to do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now bullet point 7. Could you please confirm that Mr. Siber accepted my offer for oxygen to be transported to Sarajevo, with the help of UNPROFOR? Is that the case; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we accepted that, but I don't recall that we transported oxygen to Sarajevo. I do not remember that. I do not remember that anything that we agreed upon on that matter was implemented in conformity with what was agreed upon during the meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You will see that things were implemented, and you will see how they were implemented. But before that, could the document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is already in evidence. It's P1261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 1D2139. The date is 24 January. I don't know whether the document is in evidence. 24 January, and the entire document describes a rather peaceful period. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the part that I am going to read, which is the end of bullet point 1, entitled "General Situation." Lima are the observers on the Serbian side; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] "Lima side UNMOs were called to the Blazuj Hospital to witness that two of the oxygen bottles delivered by the UNHCR were found to contain gunpowder. Once confirmed, this matter was turned over to CIVPOL." [Interpretation] Was that a normal method or normal procedure, meaning when something was observed, monitors were called to the scene to confirm the matter?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you know that transporting all this material was the responsibility of UNHCR, not the UNPROFOR. They were concerned with transporting humanitarian aid from all the parties and from the warehouses of the United Nations. I do not really remember what happened, because that was up to them to say what they -- what they found in those bottles or what was presented to them. I wasn't really aware of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, that was a very ordinary telegram, was it not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the content of the telegram seems to be ordinary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 1D2140. The date is 19 January. The time is 1815 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document and tell me whether you agree that the topic is "Alleged illegal trade and smuggling on the part of the Ukrainian Battalion"? And somebody issues an order here: [In English] "Please advise this office of the result of your investigation." [Interpretation] An order was issued for an investigation to be carried out, and somebody here asks for the feedback on the investigation; right? You did mention that you had problems with some battalions. Could you please enlighten us? What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I was informed about by the military police, that there were rumours of illegal trade in fuel exercised by the Ukrainian Battalion. Fuel was being transported to Kiseljak and surrounding areas in exchange for cigarettes and other items. It was a disciplinary issue, and I summoned the commander of the Ukrainian Battalion, and I asked that his deputy be removed from his post, if I remember correctly. It was a disciplinary issue, an internal issue, and you know that officers and soldiers tend to commit stupid mistakes in situations like this. I have taken the necessary action, and disciplinary action was taken against those who were involved in the process.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D521, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 1D2141. The date is 9 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were still there at the time. The document describes an incident that you, yourself, mentioned; the killing of Mr. Hakija Turajlic. We will briefly look at the document. Under bullet point 1, you or somebody reports from Sarajevo -- a lieutenant-colonel -- colonel reports to the Main Staff in Zagreb that: "On January 8, 1993, at about 1630 hours, the French Battalion could hear through the radio net IC that a convoy of armoured vehicles had been stopped at the Serbian check-point in Nedzarici because one passenger was not able to produce a regular pass or a UN ID card." Can we move on to the second page of the same document and look at bullet point 5. Bullet point 5 describes the unfortunate incident, and you can see clearly that the person questioned was nervously distraught. It says: [In English] "The tension was also down, and the CO just about --" commanding officer, probably, "just about to negotiate about closing the APC door, and when two or three men, very upset, tried to pull the commanding officer away from the entrance, the Serbian commander stopped them. One of them, realising that he would not succeed, stepped back, held a gun, and shot above the commanding officer's shoulder, at Mr. Hakija Turajlic, crouching in the front part of the APC. Pulled back by his commander, he got released and fired several bullets." [Interpretation] Do you remember the incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
