utterances.text: Yes, I do. That incident took place as described in the document. If an official from the Presidency wanted to move to the airport, it was our duty and we were asked to provide an armoured vehicle with an escort. Our understanding was that person would be a minister, for example, to travel to -- for an international meeting or to discuss relief operations. I, personally, was in charge of providing a number of escorts and security operations for the transport of Mr. Izetbegovic, and one day the Presidency asked us for an APC to accompany or to transport an official from the Presidency. It was mentioned it would be a minister or some high-ranking official. However, after the incident we realised it was a government delegation going to the airport to negotiate with a Turkish delegation that arrived on a relief plane to Sarajevo Airport. We wanted to be careful about that, and we knew that the presence of Turkish delegations could provoke the Serb side. And we wanted to ensure that would not be a cause for provocation, and we advised them that if they wanted to meet a Turkish delegation, that they should seek a different location. What happened? That delegation went to the airport and conducted the negotiations, and, of course, the Serb liaison officer at the airport reported to his superiors. And as Colonel Sartre of the French Battalion pointed out and described the incident by saying that the killing was intentional, was premeditated, because he was inside the armoured personnel carrier. We launched an inquiry, and we were told that a senior A2, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, would conduct the investigation. And we had that person, and we explained the sequence of events. At the time, we were criticised by the Presidency for our role, but we made it clear to them that, You did not conform to the agreement that we had, you did not tell us that -- what was the purpose of the trip. There was no escort. You did not ask for an escort. You just wanted an armoured personnel carrier, because always there was negligence on the part of the government to provide accurate information about who was travelling. We were not able to provide the requisite protection, and the outcome was the killing of this moderate member of the Presidency. However, I'd like to reiterate what Colonel Sartre said; that the person was shot intentionally, and the person who shot that individual knew what he was doing, and that that person was mentally disturbed, had a mental problem. And that's how I understood the situation to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that you understood this well. Have you heard that the International Court, with international judges and international prosecutors, set this soldier free after the war? A trial was held in Sarajevo. I assume that this was also on the basis of his mental status. Just yes or no. Have you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not follow what happened, because in the wake of the inquiry I was getting ready to leave my post in Sarajevo. But I remember I was told that the person who committed the killing was mentally disturbed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D522, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D2142. This is also the 10th of January. Obviously, as the general assessment says, it was a relatively quiet period of time. Now, we see, under number 2, that 227 people, including 207 men, were stopped and turned back by your forces while trying to cross the runway. It says here: "Egyptian Battalion, relatively quiet. "French Battalion, relatively quiet. "Ukrainian Battalion, quiet. One convoy was escorted." And so on. Can we have the next page, please. Paragraph 8, please. That's at the bottom of the page. I would like to present the first part of this paragraph briefly: [In English] "The nightly airport crossings are becoming an increasing problem. Larger numbers of people (now mostly men) are crossing. Dense fog and a new tactic of crossing in larger groups result in more people slipping past French Bat soldiers who are being overwhelmed. The danger is that as more men slip from the side to the other, the Serbs may decide that UNPROFOR is unable to stop the flow of potential fighters and intervene with the fire ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that your officer also assessed that Serbs could worry if so many men are being taken across the runway and that this may be a question of manoeuvres by future combatants?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, to my exact and accurate knowledge, that families were split up and there were attempts to reunite themselves with other members of their families on the other side of the dividing line. And I raised that issue with General Galic. He told me that if this were to continue, the crossing attempts were to continue, then UNPROFOR should take the appropriate measures to prevent that from happening, and that if the crossings continued, he would find himself in a position to continue to fire. And that's what he told me. So I conveyed that view to the Presidency, and I told them that there is a need for the Presidency to take strict measures. I made them aware that this is causing problems with the other side and is endangering the lives of those who are trying to cross. And there were several civilians. I remember there was a lady with a baby met her death on the tarmac of the airport, and this understandable in a hostile environment like this. I know that the French Battalion took the brunt of these crossings, and I told the Presidency that it is difficult to tell whether those who are trying to make the crossing are civilians or military personnel and they were trying to get to -- in the direction of the Butmir area. And I remember I spoke with the commander on the -- in the Butmir area, and I believe at one point we managed to put an end to these crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was possible for civilians to cross over to the other side, provided there was notification given, and with the assistance of UNPROFOR? However, so many people crossing, almost 300, and under foggy conditions, that seemed to be different. Do you agree that UNPROFOR often provided security for convoys going to Split and to Belgrade? Do you remember that civilians could get through if they applied a different procedure?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we did not evacuate any civilians from Sarajevo to Split, except for the students, foreign students, who were -- who found themselves trapped in Sarajevo, and their embassies asked for the UN's help. As far as other civilians, we did not have the authority. We did not have any instructions to move people from one area to the other. We did not -- we were not involved. We were not implicated in any such operations, but I know that both sides were accusing us of doing this. But I can assure you what we did was we undertook to evacuate foreign students trapped in Sarajevo, and their embassies, their delegations, asked us to help with their evacuation. At the time, General Nambiar asked me to contact the various parties, the various sides, to secure the evacuation of those foreign students. I did that. I met with Ms. Plavsic, and she gave the authorisation for the evacuation move. And we used a private company, in co-ordination with the government, to provide coaches to transport the students with UN escorts. And upon the return of the escort force, they reported to me that the three drivers of the three coaches were removed from the driver's seat by Serb forces and they were asked -- and Serb drivers -- or the three different drivers were driving the coaches. We could not trace of three drivers. And you remember very well that we raised the issue with you and with Ms. Plavsic, and we never got a clear-cut response. And the last time I met with Ms. Plavsic, she told me, General, you're talking about three drivers, and I am talking about hundreds of my people. Why so much emphasis on the three drivers? And I said to her, Madam, we are looking at drivers who were under the escort -- under the protection of the united force. I will note down what you tell me and I will take that to my superiors. But she did not give me an indication of the whereabouts or the fate of the drivers. I have an addition also to make, Mr. Karadzic. You told me that these individuals were fighting in Igman, and you told me they have gone to Split and then to Zagreb. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember that, General, they had been captured in reconnaissance operations, and later on they were exchanged for Serb combatants. However, they were asked to leave Bosnia so that they would not go back to fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D369, could we have that briefly, please, just to see this letter of mine to General Morillon from December 1992 that pertains to these requests to release civilians. Therefore, we're not going to dwell on the letter for a very long time, because it's self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this? It's the 6th of December, 1992. This is what I say in the first paragraph: [In English] "During last weeks, the ill-treatment has received such a form and degree that the Serbian young men are being forced, by brutal means or physical violence, to joint the Muslim Army." [Interpretation] The second paragraph: [In English] "No more than 100.000 Serbs have been ethnic hostages in the cities or town under the Muslim authorities." [Interpretation] And there's a description of all the things that they were experiencing. Could we have the next page, please. It's the second paragraph on the second page. I am recalling the agreement that we had signed in London in the month of July enabling civilians to move freely: [In English] "In agreement on free circulation of civilians (which is provided by the Geneva Conventions) was reached at the London Conference, and all three sides signed it in Geneva on October the 2nd, 1992. But it has not been respected so far ..." [Interpretation] And so on. And further down, it says: [In English] "The Presidency and the government of Republika Srpska brought a decision on December the 1st, 1992, to present you a demand for the urgent and obligatory rendering possible for all those who wish it, regardless of nationality, to cross to the Serbian territory - Grbavica ..." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Do you remember that we kept asking for that all the time; namely, that civilians from Sarajevo be allowed to leave the city if they so wish, and that we opened corridors for Slovenes, Jews, Muslims, who crossed our territory in order to reach Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you know the problem of the United Nations in this matter. We were not allowed at all to cater to such a request. It was very clear, and you did not bring this up, that this is ethnic cleansing. But how does the world understand it? How do we understand it? If you ask that the Serbs move out from inside Sarajevo, others will understand that this is so that you will destroy the city, with all those who remain in it after you evacuate the city. So there is a case of uncertainty on the other side, in the adversary. Therefore, everybody was highly tense, and we were trying to ask them to stop the firing first and then we will decide who goes where. Stop the shelling of civilians first. This is what concerned us first and foremost, as well as the international community. Freedom of mobility was for people -- was it for people to move according to ethnic divisions? This is what Ms. Plavsic asked me, for the evacuation of 500 people. I told her, Please don't ask us for such requests. I do not have the mandate for this. Please drop this point. Let us not raise it again. We are not in a situation to do so. Yet I noticed that within Sarajevo, there were good relations amongst some people, and there were relations of fear among others. There are those who were afraid, and they came to the UN headquarters to seek protection. And we would tell them, We do not have the mandate to do this. And we were accused by the Bosnian government to be overseeing the ethnic cleansing process, and we told them, No, these people are in fear, and we are allowing them -- am I too quick and are the interpreters able to catch up with me or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are very fortunate to be able to follow, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thanks to the excellence of our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in this document, General, you do see that I said "regardless of nationality," and sometimes, say, Macedonians and Slovenes asked to move out collectively, the Jewish organisation, this British Jewish organisation, had signed an agreement with me to make it possible for them. Do you agree with me, General, that the Geneva Convention prohibits ethnic cleansing, but also the taking of ethnic hostages; that is to say, prohibiting the freedom of movement of civilians? I just need a yes or no on that.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course -- as far as the Geneva Conventions, of course, ethnic cleansing is completely prohibited in all these conventions. However, on the freedom of mobility under war conditions, we noted that what was needed here was mobility on ethnic grounds, and this is what we refused. And this is the detail I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. These are absolutely -- this is absolutely not criticism of UNPROFOR, but the other side that kept Serbs and others, including Muslims, as you wrote in your reports, or your people wrote in these reports, that what was there was the promotion of a siege mentality. That's the picture they were trying to create. And I called these civilians who are being kept there ethnic hostages. Do you remember that I talked about that all the time, that it's much better to be an ethnic refugee than an ethnic hostage, because a refugee is at least temporarily safe, whereas hostages were always faced with the danger of something happening to them? Do you remember that in addition to ethnic refugees, I introduced this term "ethnic hostages," and that I thought that that was just as impermissible as ethnic cleansing was?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I recall is that the movement of certain ethnic groups, though the request was put on humanitarian grounds, but I told you, Please appreciate our position. We are acting under the eyes of the whole world, and our guide-lines, our regulations, do not allow us. Perhaps this is an exceptional situation that relates to the particular situation in Bosnia in general, and, of course, the United Nations guarantees freedom of mobility, but not under conditions of war, when the situation is as it was in those days. Such mobility -- such a displacement would bring danger upon them and would undermine the credibility of the United Nations, as well as increasing the tensions of hostilities in the crisis zones, to perpetuate them and to make them even more hotter and more undermining of international security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you will have 10 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Didn't you say until 1.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I gave you an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then that's the interpretation I received, until 1.00 p.m., until 1.00. Thank you. Can this be admitted? So that is what I expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, since I have only 10 minutes left, could I ask you for a brief clarification of certain concepts so that the Trial Chamber would understand what we mean when we say certain things. Can we spend these 10 minutes just having yes-or-no answers. Do you agree that your reports to the UN were accessible to the co-chairman on the Conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina; one of the co-chairman was always there on behalf of the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not my own reports, in particular, but the reports of the higher leadership in Zagreb. When the reports were from Sarajevo or other areas, these were drafted into the overall report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what I had assumed. So it was a synthetic report, as it were, that was sent to the United Nations and was accessible to all. Do you agree that before the war and during the war, we were involved in a peace process at some international conference, one or another?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that you mentioned that we also handed over some maps to you, maps that explained what was acceptable to us as a political solution, especially with regard to territories?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, such a map was there at the meetings of Mr. Nambiar with the sector command, and we believe they did not reflect our point of view. They did reflect your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, our point of view. Do you agree that we were under constant pressure to accept solutions that we fought against, and they were not favourable for us, in the territorial sense, and also in the sense that they envisaged a very strong central government?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are dragging me into a political discussion. Now, what I know, from my experience, is that if there is a true desire for peace, then the parties have to meet in the middle of the way. Nobody gets all that he wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree concessions have to be made. I don't want to drag you into a political discussion. I just wish to inform the OTP and the Trial Chamber that when we talked to you, we hoped that the synthetic reports from Zagreb would be available to the co-chairman and that the co-chairman would suggest solutions that we would not be able to accept for the reasons of territories and the constitutional reasons. We opposed to those solutions. And the way you portrayed it was that we were constantly opposed to the central government. Do you remember that; yes or no? I'm sure that you will remember.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, will you allow for the possibility that we may have not been clear enough, and thus we contributed to the confusion and to the misunderstanding of the sentence, We cannot live with the Croats and the Muslims? Do you accept that what we meant to say was that we could not live under the Croats and Muslims or, rather, under the central or centralised unitarian government which was under the control of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you of the fine meeting we had at Christmas, and I asked you, What's your bottom line? And you said, and this was a side talk -- we were not in a professional meeting, I was not on a professional mission. It was a social and humanitarian occasion. And I heard from you and your members this particular expression, We cannot living together anymore. They said this. And they said, Why not? Get your lessons from the world. Germany invaded France and Europe, and today they are members, and the same thing in the Middle East. Between us and Israel, there are so many issues and so much blood flowing. But here we are living and we hope that the future will be good so people do not stop at one stage and life goes on. I said this, and perhaps you recall. I hoped that you would find a certain way to do it, and I said, You have to have the political will to do so. You know that I write my diaries and I have written down such things in detail. I told you, You need the political will to do so, and then you will live together, ultimately, because there is nowhere else for you to go to. I only want to clarify my own point of view through the discussion that took place on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, General, sir, that there were little villages and little towns in Republika Srpska which were purely Muslim, and they remained intact until the very end of the war; for example, Janja and Biljana, some villages on Mount Romanija, and so on and so forth? Do you remember that there were such villages? Those villages that did not get involved in the fighting remained intact until the very end of the war? Just yes or no to the question. Whether you remember that there were such villages?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, and I underline this. I want to clarify a matter. When we would discuss the conditions in Zagreb, the hot spots or the hot places where clashes were taking place were defined, as well as the peaceful places, and then each sector commander would clarify the situation. In fact, there were some safe areas where there were no problems that the United Nations had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General, sir. I wish I'd been clear when it came to explaining our position. When I said that we could not live together, I meant that we could not live under the central government. But I believe that I've rectified that. Your Excellencies, I have finished my cross-examination. If the OTP does not object to the associated documents of the United Nations, I would like to tender those into evidence as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Associated with what, Mr. Karadzic; with his amalgamated statement or what else document you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I primarily mean the United Nations document from that period, the original telegrams, or our letters to them covering the topics that the general testified about in the courtroom. We would like to be given the possibility to use associated documents which are not in dispute, without having to waste any courtroom time on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Speaking for myself, those are proper -- an appropriate subject for a Bar table motion, but we'll consider whatever motions will be filed from you, Mr. Karadzic. And before I give the floor to you, the Chamber has some questions for the witness, starting from Judge Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. I should like to take you back to the evidence you gave yesterday, and we would like certain areas to be clarified. What I shall do is to read a portion of the testimony to assist you in putting it in context. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and Dr. Karadzic, this is page 5537 of yesterday's transcript, lines 8 to 14. Now, General, in answer to Dr. Karadzic, you said: "I said that that was my personal feeling. Nobody prompted me or nobody alluded to me about that. So with all the shelling and the deprivation the civilians were facing, and not seeing any glimmer of hope after the presence of the UN forces, that led me to the conviction or to the belief that the civilians wanted international intervention, wanted the international community to step in. Nobody told me this, but that was how I felt." Now, who wanted the international community to step in, the SDA leadership or the civilians?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I said this was my personal feeling. Nobody talked with me about their desire in any formal way for an international intervention. Nobody said this to me, but I -- due to the fact that I was present, I had lots of contacts and discussions; many people, journalists, officials, and ordinary people, even, came to the PTT building, or when I met them while I was on a visit here or there. We would sit and talk in order for me to discover what were the feelings of people. And people found out that we were under attack, just as the civilians were. They did not find, in the presence of the United Nations, sufficient protection. We did not provide them with sufficient protection from shelling, or we did not provide them with the necessities of life. And the media conducted a vicious campaign against us, and they accused us of this. They said we were not qualified, and unable to move, and they considered us to be victims. And we considered ourselves, as well, to be victims. And in my reply to them, I said, Yes, we are suffering. We left our beautiful and calm and good lives in our countries and came here and we live under the same situation. So this was my personal feeling. I felt they wanted something else, something more effective, something that would bring them security and safety and put an end to this situation, this inhumane situation full of bloodshed and killing. This was the feeling I got, and I -- in my meeting with the Secretary-General, I told him that this was the feeling. I told him, People are desperate here and they believe we are not effective, not efficient. And I believe there was a need for international pressures in order to arrive at a political solution, for with the shelling going on, we would not reach a solution at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you very much, indeed, for that, General. Now, Ms. Retzlaff, Dr. Karadzic, I now refer to page 5575, lines 4 to 19. Now, General, again yesterday Dr. Karadzic said: "In conversation, the French officers emphasised that Muslim forces have been responsible for many attacks on UN forces in Sarajevo. They also claim that the Bosnian leadership keeps water supplies limited to strengthen the siege mentality and to make the city the focus of international attention." And Dr. Karadzic asked you: "Do you remember that this is what we were saying all along, and that we were disbelieved until the representatives of the international community saw this for themselves?" You asked for a bit of clarification, and then he continued: "Well, the question -- we were saying that the Muslims were playing tricks on us and that they wanted us to be accused of victimising the city, as the French people say here, to strengthen the siege mentality. However, we were not believed until the foreigners experienced this themselves." Now, you did answer the question, General, but can you, please, for my benefit -- do you remember that this was what the Serb side was saying all along, that they were disbelieved until the representatives of the international community saw it for themselves?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, answering that question, I would say that we used to deal with things case by case, as United Nations, so we would take the claims of the Serbian side to the other side and discuss it over with them. And as I said, all sides denied what they -- all the violence that they committed, and they accused the other side of starting the violence and that what they did was retaliation in order to stop the violence of the other side. We, as the United Nations -- and that is why I called the entire situation as a war game, because that war game was not conducted in compatible of warfare rules. It was a civil war. Neighbours fought their neighbours, civilians fought other civilians. So I knew the nature of the situation that I was going to be faced with, so when I went to the meetings, I had a previous knowledge of what was going to be said to me during the meetings. So if there are some facts concerning offensive acts by the Muslim side, I think I -- that would -- must have been mentioned in my reports and to the other side. I mean, that happened with the Serbian side, that I respected them, because I knew that General Galic was a soldier who acted upon orders. Of course, leaders would like to seem cooperative and would like to give a positive image of themselves, but they lacked the control. I think the first thing a leader should do or a commander should do, that a commander should exercise total control of his or her subordinates. Otherwise, there is some kind of malfunction in their duties. I hope I have answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You have, and I thank you. I have one final question for you, General. And Ms. Retzlaff and Dr. Karadzic, this is at page 5583, lines 5 and 6. Now, in answer to Dr. Karadzic, General, you said: "The bars was not from the media. The media was able to move very freely in the region. They followed events and developments." Now, General, are you saying that the media did not encounter any sort of restrictions or inhibitions in their movements in the region at any time at all?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know how the media correspondents worked. They are adventurers. They carry around their cameras and they receive high salaries for their work, and I think the same goes for any other place in the world where there's a conflict. So they take pictures. I raised the question with Mr. Karadzic. I told him that, You were bringing damage and prejudicing your own cause. What you're doing is before the eyes and ears of the entire world. The media correspondents are everywhere, and they convey that image to the world. And I think the media has a strong impact on developments. They have strong weapons to do so. And I told the Serbs that they failed in their mission to change their image. I apologise. I -- Christiane Amanpour approached me for an interview. I said, Well, accepting or giving interviews to media was contrary to the rules observed by the United Nations. And she asked for an interview with Mr. Karadzic. I facilitated her transport, and she could communicate with him. I also asked her to interview Mr. Ganic. Mr. Izetbegovic was out of town. So nobody can question the role of media. We, as commanders, cannot stand in their way, so we wouldn't cause any hindrance to the movement of CNN correspondents, for example, who carried cameras around. They also have their own bypass -- bypasses where they can get to their objective according to their own methods. I personally received some training, media training. So if you are asking the question whether the media has an impact on the world public opinion, I say, Yes. So why would the media focus on the Serbian party? I think it is their own choice, their own affair. So I think that we know we are all -- we are all influenced by the media. Some people would use the media to diffuse reports or to broadcast reports, but we do not follow the media. We have our own monitors, who would report on the situation on the ground, and we report the events to our leadership and our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you. I wasn't targeting the influence of the media. But in answering the question, you gave me what I was after, and I thank you very much, indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison has a further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: General, as a very senior officer, you would have seen both success and failure in terms of command and control, in the military sense. You said, in your evidence, that subordinate officers in the field didn't comply with the aspirations of the commanders when you had talked to them face to face, and you said that, effectively, on a number of occasions. Bearing in mind your own experience as a senior officer, and your specific experience in Sarajevo, did you see that as more a deliberate failure of goodwill by the subordinates or a lack of effective command and control through the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to assess that situation from a professional standpoint, I think we -- we can accept both possibilities. I know that there are militias -- there are civilians who work alongside the military, who are trained how to use a gun and how to fire a gun. But as for the discipline and rules of engagement that should be observed by the subordinates, and their obeying of the orders, I think that was loose on the ground. In my talk with the leadership, with the commanders, I urged them to make more efforts to that direction. If that happened, I think many achievements could have been made, and, I know that have you a good intention to co-operate with the United Nations, but you have failed to control your subordinates. And I know the situation was of a civil war. There were militias, there were soldiers, there were civilians who carried weapons and who were armed with strong passions, and were urged to fight side by side their soldiers, so I think those people were not trained on the rules of engagement. I think there was some failure in the communications system or some failure in the chain of command. So I think in order to evaluate the situation, I think there was a lack of control by the central command and that there was no full co-ordination between the leadership and the higher command and the subordinates on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Arabic spoken]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Retzlaff, do you have some questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, actually I do have a question in relation to an answer that was given on page 56 -- sorry, 57, the last bit from line 16 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in relation to the discussion of whether people in Sarajevo, in particular, the Serbs, were taken hostage, you gave the following answer: "I noticed that within Sarajevo, there were good relations among some people and there were relations of fear among others. There are those who were afraid, and they came to the UN headquarters to seek protection." General, those that came to the UN headquarters to seek protection, what were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear madam, I think the continued shelling of the city, the sniping -- continued sniping, lack of supplies, I think all those factors led those people -- well, of course, the endurance can be relative. So I think those were the reasons that determined the morale of the population. So people did not have any problem of living together. They wanted the United Nations to bring about a cessation -- a cessation of hostilities. And I can say that we hired the services of civilians and those to help us with our mission, and the civilians were a mixture of Croatians, Serbians, and Bosnians. We used to throw parties in the presence of all these ethnic representatives of the ethnic groups. So the overall feeling among those people was their will to bring about a cessation of hostilities. So I wanted to bring about the full implementation of the agreements that were reached with the parties. I know that the people of Sarajevo wanted to live together, and there was no doubt about that. I said that I asked Ms. Plavsic not to ask me to help to displace individuals on ethnic basis, and that shouldn't be -- and the United Nations shouldn't be asked to do so. I hope I have been clear enough on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you, General. Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. There's just one issue that came up during the last portion of his testimony that I'd like to bring to the attention of the Chamber. I'm sorry to prolong the proceedings at this point. On page 62, and lines 15 and 16, he said: "You know, I have my diaries, and I have written things down in detail." In response to a question about a meeting he had at Christmas with Dr. Karadzic. And I was wondering if the Chamber would be willing to inquire of the general whether, after redacting any personal information, he would be willing to make those diaries, for this period that he served in Sarajevo, available to the Chamber to assist the parties in obtaining further details that might assist us in coming to the truth in this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you have any observation to this comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if you want me to send to you a diary, I think there are notes about so many years contained in that diary -- I always write down what happens in the world, and I noted down everything that happened. From a military point of view, I note down articles, press articles, and other things. And I can assure you that I published a number of articles. I never talked about the situation there. I would talk about the military difficulties that I would be faced with, so those -- that is the kind of articles I would publish. If you want me to give you that, a copy of that, I would go to my library and make a collection of those articles and send you those articles. I told you that I talked about a particular document. I commented a particular document that was shown on the screen. All what I mentioned in that diary was compatible about what was shown on the screen. I have no problem in sending you that diary. You would find notes about my mission in Angola, about my meetings in Angola with the Angolan president or the commander of the UNITA movement. I would scribble some notes about those meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to clarify that, actually, we would just be asking for this time-period that he was in Sarajevo, and also for him to exclude anything that was personal in nature. So it could be very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm noting the time. I leave it at that. So I would like to advise the parties, if necessary, to liaise with the Victim and Witness Section, to contact with the witness, whether he would be willing to copy those parties, redacting those unnecessary parts, and pass it on to the other parties. Thank you, General. This concludes your evidence, and the Chamber wishes to express gratitude to you for your coming to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Mr. President. And I thank all the parties, and I wish you all success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Suljevic. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Karadzic, you have a new member or an expert to introduce to the Bench?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you for giving me this possibility to introduce Zorica Subotic from Belgrade. She's the Defence expert for this particular area, this segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Madam Subotic. Mr. Gaynor, now it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you state --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Ekrem Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the 9th of February, 2010, you signed an amalgamated witness statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 22267 be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, yesterday the statement was read to you in its entirety in your language, and you looked at the underlying documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During your review, you noted one or two minor errors and a couple of minor clarifications which you wished to make; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I simply propose to read the six minor corrections to the consolidated statement and ask the witness to -- if he agrees with that. In paragraph 1, change "Stanislav Galic" to "Dragomir Milosevic." In paragraph 8, line 2, move the words "Mirza Jamakovic" to, after the words "the head of our department." In paragraph 17, line 5, delete the words "and the flight." Paragraph 17, line 7, insert the words "the location from which the projectile had been fired," after the word "observed." In paragraph 48, at the last line, change the word "shell" to "primary charge." The heading before paragraph 49, the date should read "24th of May," not "26th of May." And the document referred to in paragraph 58 should be "65 ter 09796," rather than "09818."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, subject to those corrections, Mr. Suljevic, do you confirm that your amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence and that you would provide the same answers to questions if you were asked, under oath, about those topics today?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully, to the best of my knowledge and my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I seek to have the amalgamated statement admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I propose to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence set out in that statement. Ekrem Suljevic is a mechanical engineer and was an investigator for the Counter Sabotage Protection Unit, or the KDZ, of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the RBiH MUP, which was tasked with the investigation of serious shelling incidents at civilian locations during the siege of Sarajevo. He participated in the investigation of 50 to 60 such incidents. In his amalgamated statement, he discusses reports by the RBiH MUP KDZ and the Sarajevo Security Services Centre, or CSB, of the RBiH MUP in respect of 17 shelling incidents in Sarajevo from December 1994 to July 1995. He explains the methodology of the RBiH MUP KDZ when investigating shelling incidents, including determining the direction of fire and the collection and analysis of projectile fragments. He explains the markings on projectile fragments which indicate the year in which they were manufactured and the location of manufacture, which in many cases was the Krusik factory in Valjevo in Serbia. He also discusses the structure of modified air-bombs, which were bombs designed to be dropped from aircraft which were crudely modified in order to be delivered by a rocket system and were, therefore, highly inaccurate weapons. That ends the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Suljevic, during the period you were working in the KDZ in 1994 and 1995, could you describe briefly, in general terms, the level of intensity of shelling in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo was shelled intensely. There were days when there was a relative lull. While we worked, we were actually over-worked in the beginning, because the CSB asked us to take part in investigations that were investigations of incidents that were caused by projectiles falling, regardless of whether there were any casualties involved. Sometimes, we could not even take part in this because we were so busy. After that, it was suggested, or agreed, if I can put it that way, that our employees should be called by the CSB only in investigation cases when there were casualties involved when a projectile exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Suljevic, in your statement you've described, and that's at paragraphs 37 to 40, the concept of modified air-bombs. Just briefly summarise what a modified air-bomb consisted of.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, a modified air-bomb - that's what we called it, at least - is a structure that consists of an air-bomb that is intended, as the name says, itself, for aircraft use. It was propelled by rocket engines, and these two parts are connected through an adapter, so that it would be a compact whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've also referred in your statement, paragraph 29, to the fact that your unit collected unexploded projectiles which had been fired upon Sarajevo, and you retained those for research. Could you give us a few examples of the kinds of projectiles which your unit collected and retained?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, we were not involved in collecting them. But when we would learn of such projectiles, our unit would remove them. The explosive charge would be removed, and the remaining parts of the projectiles would be left as samples in order to compare the traces that we saw during investigations after explosions. So -- well, I haven't been in that department since 2003, but to this day there are such samples in that department, from the very smallest ones, 60-millimetre mortar projectiles, to 155-millimetre projectiles. Also, there are samples of fuses. I actually found this when I came to the department. I think that as the JNA was leaving the barracks and the school centre there, I think that that's when those samples were brought in. That's where I found them, and they are there to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: From your statement, Mr. Suljevic, it appears that you're familiar with projectiles such as 120-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars, 76-millimetre artillery projectiles, and 155-millimetre Howitzer shells, just by way of example; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Suljevic, on Monday, as you'll remember, I showed you 45 documents, and you provided observations on those documents. Now, I propose to take you very swiftly through those documents and to ask you to tell the Court your observations on those documents as concisely as you possibly can, please. And so we'll start. If I could ask that 65 ter 06923 be brought up? Now, Mr. Suljevic, you'll remember, if we just pass quickly to pages 2 and 3 of this document in the B/C/S version - there's just one English translation - now you'll remember that essentially the content of all three documents are the same. So if we just focus on the one that's on your screen now, could you just quickly describe what that document is, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a telefax message that was sent by the director of Pretis, a company that is in Vogosca. Throughout the war, it was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. The director is asking the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to speak to the chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia so that he can receive 1.000 rocket engines, 122, for -- Grad, and that that be sent to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Suljevic, the reference to 122-millimetre Grad rockets there appears to coincide with references in paragraph 51 and 53 of your statement to the use of 122-millimetre Grad rockets for the delivery of modified air-bombs. Does this appear to be the same kind of rocket as we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it's the same rocket engines, 122 millimetres. It's called "Grad."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to the next document, which is 07123.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you can read that, Mr. Suljevic. And can you just briefly tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Dragomir Milosevic, is sending a document to some brigade, some 3rd Brigade. Pursuant to the order of the chief of General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the following is ordered: Out of the total of 2.648 rounds of 82-millimetre mortar which came from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the 27th Logistics Base, probably, should return 1.000 rounds of 82-millimetre mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the 82-millimetre mortar, is that the same kind of projectile that you've described in your statement as being one of the kinds used in shelling incidents which you investigated as part of your work for the KDZ?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in every report that involved 82-millimetre shells, it was those shells. I don't know which shells you are referring to specifically, but there were reports that pertained to 82-millimetre shells because there are no other shells for 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Suljevic. If we can have the next document, which is 07239. At this stage, Your Honours, I'd like to request if you'd prefer if I tender each document individually or if I tender them when I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it would be okay, given the situation, to tender them comprehensively at the end of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this document, Mr. Suljevic, if you can focus not -- just on the opening words of the document and then, for example, on the items described in numbers 9, 10, and 11. Tell us briefly what this document is.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This document, issued by the commander of the Sarajevo Drina Corps, was sent to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army, asking them to refer to the Army of Yugoslavia with a request for a further batch of weapons and ammunition. Under numbers 10, 11 and 12: 200 shells for 120 mortars; 76-millimetre shells for M42 ZIS gun; 82-millimetre shells for MB; and, finally, 300 rounds of 155-millimetre shells for M1 Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do these coincides with the kinds of projectiles which you or your unit recovered from locations in Sarajevo following their firing upon Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all those three types of projectiles were kept in our department as samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like the next document to be brought up, please. That's 07403.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a notification signed by Zarko Ljubojevic, who was authorised by the head of the Logistics Sector, or, rather, its technical department. And in this notification, we see that the following types and quantities of aerial bombs will be given for completion: 15 pieces of FAB-100; 40 pieces of FAB-250; and also motors for 128-millimetre rocket, a total of 57 pieces, plus three handwritten [as interpreted], which amounts to the grand total of 60 pieces. And further on, it says -- or, rather, there are instructions as to how the aerial bombs should be completed, and it says here that FAB-100 should be completed with one motor each, whereas FAB-250 should be completed with three motors each.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What do you understand the term "completed" means in this context?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Within this context, this means to make a modified aerial bomb which will have the explosive charge of an aerial bomb, and that it will be adapted to include a motor which will carry the charge from the moment the bomb is launched to the moment it lands at its target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have 08136, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, focusing, really, just on the first paragraph of this document, as well as its header, just tell us what this one's about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Technical Overhaul and Repairs Institution, based in Hadzici, which was under the control of the VRS Army throughout the entire war, sent a request to the Ilijas Ironworks and refers to an order of the Main Staff of the VRS, and the request is for six pieces of six-metre-long launchers, and the launchers will be used to produce launchers for the modified aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain how you deduced that they'll be used for modified air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: They will not be used for the aerial bombs or modified aerial bombs. They will be used for the launching pads for such aerial bombs. From those pads, modified aerial bombs would be launched or fired in the direction of a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have 08146, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Suljevic, focusing your attention, really, on the last sentence of the first paragraph, as well as on items 3, 6, 7, and 8, could you tell the Court what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps requests from the Main Staff of the VRS to prepare an approval, and that approval would be taken by their representative to the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in order to obtain the following ordnance. And the ordnance includes: Mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, 10 pieces; 76-millimetre shells for the ZIS gun, 1.000 pieces; 800 shells for 128 millimetre; and, finally, 120-millimetre shells for a -- mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just focusing on the last couple of words of the first paragraph, could you tell the Court what you understand those to refer to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the ordnance is indispensable: "... for combat activities, especially for strengthening our front on the inner and outer rings." And since we are talking about the Sarajevo and Romanija Corps, I believe that the needs concerned combat activities on the inner and outer rings of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we have document 0484 -- pardon me, 08223, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And this one, Mr. Suljevic, could you tell us what the document is? And focus on item 1 of the listed items.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we getting the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, I'm not receiving it either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Suljevic, if you could repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps submits information to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, referring to a document issued by the Main Staff of the VRS in which they probably had requested certain information, and he also submits information about the available ordnance and equipment. Under 1, he says that they have four pieces of launchers for aerial bombs of 105, 200, and 250 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we have 04080, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is, Mr. Suljevic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the Technical Department of the Logistics Sector of the Main Staff of the VRS informs the Command of the 35th Logistics Base, as well as the Command of the 27th Logistics Base, I suppose, and also the company Pretis for information only, and it says that the 35th Logistics Base will transport, by their own transport means, and deliver to Pretis for completion the following types and quantities of aerial bombs: FAB-100, 15 pieces; and FAB -- 14 pieces. That's FAB UK7 221, as well as motors for 128 -millimetre rockets, 60 pieces. What follows are instructions as to how to complete or, rather, how to construct modified aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have 09095, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: With this document, Mr. Suljevic, could you concentrate and tell us briefly what it is? And focus on the first item listed only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the chief of artillery sent information to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps -- or, rather, he requests information about the number of launchers for aerial bombs and description as to what types of bombs each of them could launch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for the next document, which is 09102.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you comment on this document, please?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps requests from the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army to send them aerial bombs, because they needed them to enhance the combat readiness of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps units. They requested 100 pieces of FAB-100 aerial bombs as well as 100 pieces of aerial bomb FAB-250.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could you comment on the location named there in the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that: "We inform you on this occasion that we will provide for the return of the approved assets through company Krusik-Namenska, Valjevo, through our previous financial regulations of relations with the mentioned company and their possibilities to supply the aforementioned."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your amalgamated statement, you've referred to Krusik, Valjevo, in another context. What context was that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Valjevo-based Krusik was often found as marks on the remains of projectiles, which indicated that the devices had been produced in the Valjevo-based Krusik company. As far as I know, the same company, Krusik, developed and manufactured rockets, projectiles, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have 09115, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you focus, really, on paragraph 2 of this one, please, Mr. Suljevic? The original is -- if we just wait a moment, the original will be on your screen. If you look at paragraph 2 of this document and the header, just tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that we have the English match. The Logistics Sector of the Main Staff of the VRS refers to an order of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, and sends this document to the Commands of the 27th Logistics Base and the 35th Logistics Base, as well as Pretis company, for the information of the last two. And it says here that the 27th Logistics Base will collect and transport 30 pieces of FAB-100 aerial bombs and 20 pieces of FAB-250 M79 aerial bombs from the 35th Logistics Base. After the collection, the bombs, together with the corresponding number of rocket-launchers, are to be transported and delivered to Pretis HD for completion. In this case, I believe that this means completion and production of the corresponding number of modified aerial bombs. And further on, we see instructions as to how the bombs should be completed and how many engines should be -- or motors should be attached to each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have document 09162, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's a fairly short one, Mr. Suljevic. If you'd just describe briefly -- no read to read it out. Just describe, briefly, what it is.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is just a response from one of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps units, or, rather, a report on the situation with regard to aerial bomb launchers, and they say that they have just one air-bomb launcher in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Number 09185, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you tell us what this document is about? You can concentrate on the typewritten text, please.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps sends this document to the commander. This is a document in which they inform him that in Hadzici, the aerial bomb-launcher for bombs up to 500 kilometres [as interpreted] was manufactured in Hadzici of a much higher quality than any of the previous ones, which means that there were launchers before; that the launcher was mounted on a vehicle, and that a commission should be set up to carry out the testing of the technical performances of that launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Suljevic, the interpretation I heard said "500 kilometres." Was that what you intended or it might have been an interpretation error?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I said "500 kilograms." Aerial bombs of up to 500 kilograms. If I said "kilometres," it was an error, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Could I have 09186.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is -- again, this is a similar notification as you've described earlier. Just briefly describe what it is, please.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for logistics submits the requested data to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps about the equipment in their possession, including the information about aerial bomb launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have 09218, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask you to describe, just briefly, who this is to and from. And focus on the first of the four points listed in this document.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the chief of artillery, whose name is Tadija Manojlovic, for the Command of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade. It is supposed to carry out all preparations for the manufacture of one launcher by securing vehicles, rails, cranes, and other necessary means for the development of that piece of equipment, and that should be done in the Maintenance and Repairs Depot in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Next document, please, which is 09227.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you just describe what this document is, please, Mr. Suljevic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The document was sent by the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the 27th Logistics Base, and we can see in this document that the issuing of 30 aerial bombs of 105 kilograms and 200 [as interpreted] pieces of 250-kilogram aerial bombs has been approved. And we can see how the completed aerial bombs -- or, rather, modified aerial bombs should have been distributed across the units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's sufficient, thank you. Next document, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Suljevic, did you say 200 pieces of 250-kilogram aerial bombs or 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then line 2 of page 89 should read "20."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next document, Mr. Suljevic, is 09241. Again, somewhat similar to a couple of previous notifications that you've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just tell us, briefly, what it is. It will be on your screen in just a second.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: One of the units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is providing requested information to the command. Inter alia, they say that they have a launcher for air-bombs of 100 and 250 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is 09267.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you read this document and tell us your -- what you consider it to be?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In my view, this is a kind of warning of the chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It is sent to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and it says that lower-ranking units are not allowed to address them directly. That is to say, they are not allowed to address the Main Staff directly, but all this has to be done through the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. This is being issued because the Ilijas Brigade directly addressed the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to take air-bombs from the Pretis company, and they did not go through the Sarajevo Romanija Corps when they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. The next document is 09273.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this is? And also just focus on the last sentence in the order.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is writing to the Command of the Ilidza Brigade, and it is hereby ordered: that this brigade prepare a launcher with at least five aerial bombs; that the launchers be directed at the airport; and that they be ready to open fire at the command of the commander, Dragomir Milosevic. This same document strictly forbids the use of these weapons without the order of the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is 09313.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in this document, if you can tell who it is addressed to, to the best of your knowledge, please say so.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, and in my view, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is sending this document to the commands of different corps. I don't know exactly what all of these abbreviations stand for. "KK," may that be the Krajina Corps, perhaps? I'm just guessing. I see here it says "SRK," which is probably the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and some other units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Focusing on the first of the four items in respect of which they are requesting information, what does it refer to there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: What is indispensable is information, so they are requesting information concerning the number of aerial bomb launchers; by type of launcher, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 09317.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is somewhat similar to a document that you commented on earlier. Could you tell us, briefly, what this one is?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that refers to an order issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it says that the chief had regulated the transfer of aerial bombs to the Pretis company for their completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Further down the document, can you -- is there any information there which enlightens you as to what "completion" means?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Completing rocket bombs with, well, these modified air-bombs that we referred to at some point when we started.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is document 09337.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Quite similar to notifications you've commented on earlier. Tell us, briefly, what it is when it comes up.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: As was stated a moment ago, this is a response to a request to provide information about resources available, inter alia, where launchers for aerial bombs are referred to. The 1st Romania Infantry Brigade Command is saying that they don't have a single rocket-launcher yet, but the manufacture of one is underway. It has to do with air-bomb launchers, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And they are providing that information to who?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a response to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. In the previous document, we saw that request of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It was somewhere in that document. The command is actually asking their subordinate units for information about available resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is 09383.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When it comes up, could you tell us who it is from, who it is to, and what it concerns? If the last line of the document could just be made visible to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. He is sending it to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It is being sent directly to the commander. He is informing them that the request of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is justified concerning the 100- and 250-kilogram aerial bombs. In a way, he is cautioning the commander that it is his duty to take all necessary security measures, to store this equipment, and to make sure that a minimal number of people know about the equipment and the purpose for which it is to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you able -- I'll move on, Mr. Suljevic. Could I have 09399, please. In this document, you'll see, again, reference to the word "completed." Could you just comment on that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It's similar to the previous one. The Logistics Sector of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is writing to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and informing them that the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps will organise the take-over and transportation of four 250-kilogram air-bombs from the Kotorac, probably, Barracks to the Pretis company so that they could be inspected, completed, and prepared for use. After that, this will be taken over and stored by the 27th, well, Logistics Base, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just comment on the words "completion" and "completed" there.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In my view in this case as well, it has to do with the manufacture or completion of a modified air-bomb that would be ready for launching from those launchers that had also been referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have 09640.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document, could you tell us who it is from, and who it is to, and what it's about? We just need to scroll down to see who it's from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The document is being sent -- well, could we have a look further down to see who it's from? It's the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska that is sending this document to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, or, rather, to the commander, personally, and it says that the Army of Republika Srpska, that is to say, the commander, rather, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, has some information to the effect that on the 26th of April, 1995, in the evening hours or during the night, the use of two air bombs is being planned against enemy targets and neighbourhoods in the area of Sarajevo. Commander Mladic is, therefore, asking the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to inform him as to whether this is correct and for what purposes this is being planned. Does it have to do with retaliation or something like that? Also, it says that if the Supreme Command issued an order to them to start combat operations and use heavy weaponry, that it is their duty to inform Commander Mladic about that; that is to say, to inform him, the signatory, Commander Mladic. However, before combat operations start in the area of Sarajevo, he asks that a detailed report be provided on plans, objectives, and targets so that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska could make an assessment thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have document 10693, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's quite a short document. If you can just indicate who it's from and what is being ordered.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This document that I saw over the past two days, like all the other documents that we've been looking at today, well, I mean, I am simply speechless. But this is what I have to say: The commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Dragomir Milosevic, is sending an order to the Ilidza Brigade to prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and to prepare the bomb for launching; to select a target either in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija, that is to say, the most profitable target where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. And then he also says that as for the implementation of this task, that Dragomir Milosevic should be informed personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, at this time in April 1995, where were Hrasnica and the Sokolovic Kolonija, and what were they?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija are neighbourhoods that were out of Sarajevo, on the other side of the runway, that is, settlements. I mean, they're parts of the town of Sarajevo, in principle. All of that belongs to the municipality of Ilidza. However, they were on the other side of the runway. Sarajevo was connected to these settlements only by this tunnel that had been built underneath the runway in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And are you able to comment as to what kind of settlements were there? What kind of -- what was the nature of the people who were in the settlements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were settlements that were under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout. The majority population was Muslim, at least at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you in a position to comment in any way as to whether they were predominantly a military population or predominantly a civilian population?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: These were civilian settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 10929.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document, could you just tell us who it's from? And focus on the first -- in fact, you can focus on the whole document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps issues an order for aerial bombs weighing 105 and 250 kilograms, as it is stated in the document. The ordnance should be issued to Major Simic by units of the Sarajevo and Romanija Corps. Major Simic will take over two more bombs from the corps reserves to another brigade, and also two other bombs should be taken over from Pretis. All of that should be done with a view to preparing a plan for the use of an air-bomb launcher. And, generally, it has to do with preparations for this action called "Talas." I don't know what action or operation that was, Talas 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have 10932, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, I'm noting the time. You have still 18-odd documents or so. How much longer would you need for your redirect -- no, I'm sorry, for your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to get through them as quickly as possible. I suppose I would need about one more hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then there's no need -- it's impossible to conclude today, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, we'll adjourn for today, and we will continue from 9.00 tomorrow. But, in the meantime, please do not discuss your evidence with anybody until it is concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
